summary: This memo specifies the Identification Protocol, formerly called the Authentication Server Protocol, which lets a server ask a remote host which user owns a particular TCP connection. It was renamed to better reflect its function. The answer is only as trustworthy as the host giving it.

eli5.summary: Imagine asking a building's front desk who made a phone call from room number three. This protocol lets one computer ask another computer which user opened a certain connection.

questions: how to identify the user of a tcp connection
how does ident find the owner of a tcp connection
subtitle: A tiny TCP service that tells you which user owns a given connection on a remote host.

tldr.problem: A server that receives a TCP connection sees only addresses and port numbers. It has no standard way to learn which user on the other host opened the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The Identification Protocol listens on TCP port 113. A client sends a line with a port pair, and the server answers with a line giving either a USERID (operating system and user identifier) or an ERROR.
tldr.outcome: The answer is only as trustworthy as the host and organization that give it. The RFC says it is meant for auditing, not for authorization or access control.

facts.label: Client wait before abandoning a query

today: RFC 1413 is listed as a Proposed Standard from February 1993 and obsoletes RFC 931. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What the Identification Protocol Does
sections.content:
The Identification Protocol (also called ident) determines the identity of the user of a particular TCP connection. Given a TCP port number pair, it returns a character string that identifies the owner of that connection on the server's system. It was formerly called the Authentication Server Protocol and was renamed to better reflect its function. It replaces RFC 931.

It is a connection-based application on TCP. A server listens on TCP port 113. Once connected, the server reads a line naming the connection of interest and sends back the user identifier. It may then close the connection or keep answering more queries.

The server should close an idle connection after a configurable time; a 60 to 180 second idle timeout is recommended. The client may close at any time, but to allow for network delays it should wait at least 30 seconds after a query before giving up.
sections.eli5: One computer calls another computer's information desk on a well-known line and asks, who is using this connection? The desk answers with a short line of text.

sections.title: Queries and Replies
sections.content:
Queries are allowed only for fully specified connections. The addresses come from the connection the query itself arrives on, so a user on address A can only ask the server on address B about connections between A and B.

A query is a line of the form <port-on-server> , <port-on-client>. The order matters: if a client on host A wants to ask about a connection that it knows locally as 23, 6191 (an inbound TELNET connection), it must ask 6191, 23, because that is how host B describes it.

The reply repeats the same port pair and adds a response type and extra information: <port-on-server> , <port-on-client> : <resp-type> : <add-info>. Examples from the RFC are 6193, 23 : USERID : UNIX : stjohns and 6195, 23 : ERROR : NO-USER.
sections.eli5: You ask using the numbers of the two ends of the call, written from the other side's point of view. The answer repeats those numbers so you know which call it is about.

sections.title: USERID and ERROR Responses
sections.content:
A response is one of two types. For USERID, the extra information is an operating system name (with an optional character set, separated by a comma), then a colon, then an identification string. If the character set is omitted it defaults to US-ASCII. Names come from the Assigned Numbers RFC, plus one special value, OTHER, for identifiers that are not a normal user ID, such as an encrypted audit token.

The identifier may use any octet except NUL, LF and CR, and spaces after the colon are part of it. For ERROR, the extra information says why the owner could not be found:

  • INVALID-PORT: a port was out of range or not a non-negative integer.
  • NO-USER: the connection is not in use or has no identifiable owner.
  • HIDDEN-USER: the owner is known but the information was withheld at the user's request.
  • UNKNOWN-ERROR: the owner cannot be determined, or the server chooses to hide the real reason. A server with that option MUST make it configurable and MUST default to returning the proper error.

Non-standard error codes must begin with X. A server may also drop the connection without replying; a premature close counts as ERROR : UNKNOWN-ERROR.
sections.eli5: The desk either says who the caller was or says why it cannot. Reasons include a wrong number, nobody is using that line, the person asked not to be named, or just do not know.

sections.title: Formal Syntax and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC gives a formal grammar. A request is a port pair followed by an end-of-line (carriage return and line feed). A port pair is two integers of 1 to 5 digits joined by a comma. Tokens are 1 to 64 characters, and an error token that starts with X is 2 to 64 characters. A user ID is 1 to 512 octets.

On white space, the text follows "be conservative in what you send and be liberal in what you accept": it is accepted anywhere except within a token, but everything after the colon following the operating system type is part of the user ID. Clients may abort if they receive 1000 characters without an end-of-line.

A server SHOULD NOT send more than 512 octets of user ID, a client MUST accept at least 512 octets, and a server MUST put the most significant part in the first 512. A character set applies only to the user ID field; everything else is US-ASCII. If a client does not recognize the returned character set, it should treat the ID as octets and show it in hex as well.
sections.eli5: There are strict rules about how long each piece may be and which characters may appear. Be strict when writing a message and relaxed when reading one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The reply is at most as trustworthy as the host that gives it or the organization that runs the host. A PC in an open lab may let a user make the protocol return any identifier they like, and a compromised host may return completely wrong information.

The protocol is not meant as an authorization or access control protocol. At best it supplies extra auditing information about TCP connections; at worst it gives misleading or maliciously incorrect answers. Using its information for anything other than auditing is strongly discouraged, and using it for access control decisions, alone or alongside other methods, may weaken normal host security.

An ident server can also reveal information that might normally be private. The RFC compares it to CallerID phone services and says that if you would not run a "finger" server for privacy reasons, you may not want to run this one.
sections.eli5: The desk can only repeat what the building tells it, and a dishonest building can lie. So it is fine for keeping a diary of who called, but not for deciding who is allowed in.
